title: Carboxylic acids & derivatives
examples: What is the general reaction when an ester undergoes hydrolysis?
Can you explain the role of acid or base in the hydrolysis of an amide?
How do I identify the functional group of an acyl chloride?

explain.say: Today we will look at some important carboxylic acid derivatives. These groups are esters, amides, and acyl chlorides. They all react with water through a process called hydrolysis.
Esters are formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid. They have the general structure RCOOR'. A simple example is ethyl acetate, which comes from ethanol and acetic acid.
Amides are formed from an amine and a carboxylic acid. They have the general structure RCONR'R''. Think of the structure in urea, which is a common example.
Acyl chlorides are very reactive derivatives. They are formed by reacting a carboxylic acid with thionyl chloride. They have the structure RCOCl. Acetyl chloride is a common example.

Now consider hydrolysis. This is the breakdown using water. Esters hydrolyze in acid or base to give a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. For example, ethyl acetate breaks down to acetic acid and ethanol.

In a real-life setting, soap manufacturing uses saponification. This is a base-catalyzed hydrolysis of fats, which are triglycerides. The base breaks the ester bonds, yielding glycerol and a salt of the fatty acid.

faq.q: What is the difference between hydrolysis in acid versus base?
faq.a: Acidic hydrolysis usually requires heating and yields the carboxylic acid. Basic hydrolysis, or saponification, is often done under conditions that favor the carboxylate salt.
asks: Does the acid or base change the products?
How do I know which condition to use for hydrolysis?

faq.q: Are acyl chlorides always more reactive than esters?
faq.a: Yes, acyl chlorides are generally much more reactive than esters. This is because the chloride ion is a better leaving group than the alkoxy group in esters.
asks: Which derivative reacts fastest with water?
Why is the chloride group so good at leaving?

faq.q: What is the role of the nucleophile in these reactions?
faq.a: The nucleophile is the electron-rich species, like water or hydroxide ion. It attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of the derivative.

faq.q: Does the reaction mechanism change when going from an ester to an amide?
faq.a: The core mechanism involves nucleophilic acyl substitution. However, amides are much less reactive than esters because the nitrogen lone pair donates electron density, stabilizing the carbonyl carbon.

faq.q: Can I use acyl chlorides to make amides?
faq.a: Yes, you can. You react the acyl chloride with the amine, often in the presence of a base to neutralize the byproduct acid.
asks: What do I add to make an amide from an acyl chloride?
Is a base always necessary when making amides this way?

facts: Acyl chlorides are highly reactive due to the excellent leaving group ability of the chloride ion.
Base-catalyzed hydrolysis of esters is known as saponification when dealing with fats.
Amides are significantly less reactive towards hydrolysis than esters because of resonance stabilization from the nitrogen atom.
The general reaction type for all these transformations is nucleophilic acyl substitution.

quiz.say: Which derivative undergoes hydrolysis under mild basic conditions to yield a carboxylate salt and an alcohol?
quiz.why: Esters are susceptible to base-catalyzed hydrolysis, yielding the carboxylate salt.

wrong.0: Carboxylic acids do not undergo hydrolysis in this manner; they are the product, not the starting material.
wrong.2: Amides are too stable; they require harsh conditions like strong acid and heat.
wrong.3: Acyl chlorides react so quickly, they often react with the solvent itself before hydrolysis can be controlled.

quiz.say: To convert a carboxylic acid into a highly reactive derivative suitable for amide formation, which reagent is typically used?
quiz.why: Thionyl chloride is a standard reagent used to convert carboxylic acids into acyl chlorides.

wrong.0: Ethanol is an alcohol and would react with the acid to form an ester, not an acyl chloride.
wrong.1: Ammonia is a nucleophile and would react with the acid to form an amide, not an acyl chloride.
wrong.3: Sodium hydroxide causes saponification, which is not the desired conversion to an acyl chloride.

quiz.say: If a reaction mixture contains an amide and is treated with strong acid and heat, what is the expected product after hydrolysis?
quiz.why: Amides require strong acid and heat for complete hydrolysis, yielding the original carboxylic acid and amine.

wrong.1: This mix of products suggests two different types of reactions occurring simultaneously.
wrong.2: The conditions are not right for forming an acyl chloride; the acid is already present.
wrong.3: The acid protonates the amine, but the carboxylic acid part must also be liberated.
